# Transcaval Access for Structural Heart Interventions: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) has transformed the management of severe aortic stenosis, but the large-caliber introducer sheaths required can preclude the procedure in patients with inadequate iliofemoral arteries. Transfemoral access is considered the standard route for TAVR; however, in some cases this access route is contraindicated, and alternative routes such as transaxillary are emerging as first-line approaches. The transcaval (TCv) vascular approach is increasingly used in TAVR in patients unsuitable for the gold-standard transfemoral approach. Transthoracic alternatives carry their own hazards: transthoracic (transapical and transaortic) access is inferior compared with femoral-artery access, perhaps in part because of the clinical features precluding femoral artery access.

## Concept and rationale

The technique was first validated preclinically by Halabi and colleagues. Because femoral artery caliber or disease precludes vascular access in a significant minority of candidates, they proposed an alternative route to the abdominal aorta for large introducer sheaths by direct puncture from the adjoining inferior vena cava, reasoning that veins are larger and more compliant than corresponding arteries, that venous decompression may avert hemorrhage in confined-space arterial perforation, and that acquired aorto-caval fistulas are not immediately life-threatening. [1] Large therapeutic devices can be introduced into the aorta via the IVC in a simple catheter procedure, and the fistula closed uneventfully despite full anticoagulation. [1]

The first human application followed in 2014. This study described the first use of caval-aortic access and closure to enable TAVR in patients who lacked other access options—percutaneous entry into the abdominal aorta from the femoral vein through the adjoining inferior vena cava. [2] Caval-aortic access entails delivering large vascular sheaths into the abdominal aorta via the femoral vein through the IVC, and the tract can be closed using nitinol occluders. [2] The physiological basis underpinning its safety is now well established: transcaval aortic access is a versatile electrosurgical technique whose relative safety derives from the recognition that interstitial hydraulic pressure exceeds venous pressure, so arterial bleeding harmlessly decompresses into the nearby caval venous hole. [3]

## Procedural planning and technique

Meticulous computed tomography (CT) planning is essential. The target must have a calcium-free window on the right wall of the abdominal aorta, close to the vena cava, free of interposed structures such as bowel or lymph nodes, and away from branches that could be obstructed by a closure device. [4,5] Targets need to be sufficiently far (approximately ≥10–15 mm) from important aortic branches to allow bailout covered stents a hemostatic landing zone, while renal veins and lumbar arteries do not need special attention, and bailout covered stents will usually occlude the inferior mesenteric artery. [3] Crossing is accomplished electrosurgically: from the femoral vein, an electrified guidewire is directed from the inferior vena cava into a snare prepositioned in the adjoining abdominal aorta, and after guidewire exchange the standard introducer sheath is advanced into the aorta, allowing retrograde TAVR. [6,7]

## Clinical outcomes

The pivotal NHLBI investigational device exemption trial established feasibility. In 100 patients (STS predicted risk of mortality 9.6%) ineligible for transfemoral and at high or prohibitive risk for transthoracic access, transcaval access was successful in 99 of 100, device success was 98 of 99, inpatient survival was 96%, and 30-day survival was 92%. [8,9] Transcaval-related bleeding was adjudicated as VARC-2 major or life-threatening in 12 of 99 patients. [8] Intermediate-term results were reassuring: 12-month mortality was 29%, there were no late major vascular complications, and CT demonstrated spontaneous closure of almost all fistulas. [10]

The European registry corroborated these findings. Data on 50 patients treated by transcaval TAVI in five European centres demonstrated that transfemoral transcaval access proved to be a feasible and safe TAVI approach for high-risk patients with severe aortic stenosis not suitable for transfemoral access. [11] A registry comparison versus transaxillary access found that stroke or TIA were significantly less common after transcaval than after transaxillary access (2.5% vs 13.2%). [12] A subsequent meta-analysis confirmed favorable results: in 8 studies with 467 patients, transcaval TAVR achieved a success rate of 98.5%, with a 30-day all-cause mortality of 6.1% and a 1-year mortality of 14.9%. [13] Comparative analyses against supra-aortic routes have also been performed. [14,15]

## Device development and broader applications

Off-label use of cardiac occluders prompted purpose-built device development. A dedicated transcaval closure device was tested because persistent aortocaval fistulae and bleeding complications were common with off-label nitinol occluders in a prospective study. [16] The technique extends beyond TAVR. Transcaval access has been performed in thousands of patients for TAVR and endovascular thoracic aneurysm repair and to avoid limb ischemia in percutaneous mechanical circulatory support. [3,17] For TEVAR, transcaval aortic access has been used in a patient with a descending thoracic aneurysm in lieu of a surgical iliac conduit. [18,19] In mechanical circulatory support, transcaval access is feasible for emergency nonsurgical implantation of the Impella 5.0 device in cardiogenic shock with small or diseased iliofemoral arteries. [20] The approach can also traverse synthetic grafts: although there was no prior experience traversing a synthetic aortic graft, a patient underwent successful traversal of a polyester aortic graft using radiofrequency energy applied from a guidewire tip. [21,22] It has additionally been combined with leaflet-laceration techniques such as BASILICA to prevent coronary obstruction. [23,24]

## Conclusion

Transcaval access has matured from a counterintuitive concept into a validated, fully percutaneous alternative for large-bore aortic access. With meticulous CT planning and adherence to established technical steps, transcaval access offers a safe, nonfemoral route for TAVR and other interventions requiring large-bore arterial access. [3] However, dissemination has been hampered by the unavailability of commercially marketed devices. [3] Ongoing standardization of best practices [25–30] and dedicated closure technology should facilitate wider adoption, particularly as the technique is applied to lower-risk and more diverse anatomies.
